Notifications  You must be signed in to change notification settings. # paudelprabesh/Hyperparameter-Tuning-In-LSTM-Network. ## Folders and files. | Name | Name | Last commit message | Last commit date |. | Latest commit   History3 Commits 3 Commits |. ## Repository files navigation. ## Hyperparameter tuning in LSTM Network. In this study, we choose four different search strategies to tune hyperparameters in an LSTM network. The dataset that we used in this experiment is the IMDB movie review dataset which contains 50,000 reviews and is listed on the official tf.keras website. Our methods are Random Search(RS), Bayesian Optimization(BO), Genetic Algorithm(GA) and Grid Search(GS). With these methods, we tune the following hyperparameters: learning rate, number of hidden units, input length and number of epochs. We attempt to answer the following research questions:. RQ1: How do the hyperparameter tuning techniques compare with each other? RQ2: Which set of above-mentioned hyperparameters yields the best results for LSTM? We obtain three best models from GA and one each from RS and BO. Using these five models, we apply GS to get the final best set of hyperparameters. Our study shows that GA gives the best result in finding the best model with AUC of 0.946. Our comparative study between RS, BO, and GA (with Grid Search) shows that GA gives the optimal hyperparameters with high validation accuracy on the test dataset. However, Random Search and Bayesian Optimization give sub-optimal results with faster training time. results.title: RNN Hyperparameter Tuning
results.content:
Title: RNN Hyperparameter Tuning
# Hyperparameter Tuning Strategies. To improve the performance of a sequence model, tuning its hyperparameters is a common and important practice. Unlike model *parameters* (like weights and biases) which are learned during training, *hyperparameters* are configuration settings specified *before* training begins. Finding a good set of hyperparameters is essential for getting the most out of your RNN, LSTM, or GRU models. Think of hyperparameters as the knobs and dials you can adjust on your model-building machine. ### Common Hyperparameters in Sequence Models. **Choice of Recurrent Unit (SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU):** As discussed in previous chapters, the type of recurrent cell itself is a hyperparameter. You start with a reasonable set of hyperparameters (perhaps based on values reported in similar studies or common defaults), train the model, evaluate its performance on a validation set, and then adjust the hyperparameters based on the results. For example, if the model is overfitting, you might increase dropout or decrease the number of units/layers. **Grid Search:** This is an exhaustive search over a manually specified subset of the hyperparameter space. You define a grid of possible values for each hyperparameter you want to tune. The algorithm then trains and evaluates a model for *every possible combination* of these values. Grid search would then train 3×2×2=123 \times 2 \times 2 = 123×2×2=12 models. While systematic, grid search suffers from the "curse of dimensionality", the number of combinations grows exponentially with the number of hyperparameters, making it computationally very expensive. **Random Search:** Instead of trying all combinations, random search samples a fixed number of combinations randomly from the specified hyperparameter space (potentially defined by distributions rather than discrete values). Research (e.g., by Bergstra and Bengio, 2012) has shown that random search is often more efficient than grid search, especially when only a few hyperparameters significantly affect performance. It's more likely to find good values for the important hyperparameters because it doesn't waste computations on testing many values for unimportant ones. Comparison of points evaluated by Grid Search and Random Search for two hyperparameters. By systematically exploring different configurations and carefully evaluating their impact, you can significantly enhance the effectiveness of your sequence models.

Title: What is a "hyperparameter" in HTM vs Deep Learning? - Lounge - HTM Forum
There is no way to parameter tune once the model is created, which is different from DL. I think that it is fair to say that if a deep network fails to converge it is fairly common to tweak parameters or even the whole model and continue. Yes, you can fiddle with some HTM parameters before training starts but you cannot after the learning commences as the configuration of the learned bits depends on them not moving in relation to the input stream; a bit position must match the related feature or it loses the meaning of that feature. You may quibble on the detail that HTM has parameters but I will agree with what @rhyolight stated that once the training starts the model configuration is frozen. it is fairly common to tweak parameters or even the whole model and continue. In the current HTM implementation (i.e. NuPIC), there’s a form of hyper-parameter tuning. Actually, the fact that the current HTM implementation (i.e. NuPIC) contains a high number of *different* hyper-parameters upsets me a little bit. All models have initial parameters that must be tuned to process digital input. The point is that HTM learns new patterns online without hyperparameter tuning. All models have initial parameters that must be tuned to process digital input. The fact that you have not tried to tweak these parameters it doesn’t imply that they are not hyper-parameters. I don’t see why tweaking these hyper-parameters would be against nature (i.e. it would be like finding the best brain to perform a certain task). I don’t see why tweaking these hyper-parameters would be against nature. The point of that sentence is that those parameters are set before the algorithms are executed (they e.g. define the structure of the architecture of the model, the learning mechanism, etc.). I just wanted to point out that, according to the knowledge of master’s student in AI, current HTM implementations, of course, have hyper-parameters, and, of course, hyper-parameters can be optimized. For the sake of the HTM world, I think you can ignore the “hyperparameters” label altogether and we can just get back to calling them model parameters.

results.title: Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning
results.content: # Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning | by Nishtha kukreti | Medium. # Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning. Bayesian Optimization is a probabilistic model-based approach for optimizing hyperparameters. Unlike Grid Search and Random Search, which blindly test different combinations, Bayesian Optimization **builds a probabilistic model of the objective function** and **intelligently selects the next set of hyperparameters to evaluate**, leading to faster and more efficient tuning. 1.   **Define the objective function**: This function maps hyperparameters to model performance (e.g., accuracy, loss). 2.   **Build a probabilistic model**: Typically, a **Gaussian Process (GP)** is used to model the function and predict the performance of unexplored hyperparameter values. 3.   **Select the next set of hyperparameters**: It uses an **acquisition function** (like Expected Improvement or Upper Confidence Bound) to balance exploration and exploitation. 4.   **Evaluate and update**: The model is trained with the selected hyperparameters, and the GP model is updated with new results. ## Implementation: Bayesian Optimization with `optuna`. Let’s tune an XGBoost model using **Optuna**, a popular Bayesian Optimization library:.

results.title: Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning
results.content: # Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Tuning. The caveats of grid search and random search and how Bayesian optimization addresses them. Hyperparameter tuning is a tedious and time-consuming task in training machine learning (ML) models. Typically, the most common way to determine the optimal set of hyperparameters is through repeated experimentation. Essentially, we define a set of hyperparameter configurations (mainly through random guessing) and run them through our model. While this approach is feasible for training small-scale ML models, it is practically infeasible when training bigger models. **Bayesian optimization** is a highly underappreciated yet immensely powerful approach for tuning hyperparameters. It revolves around the idea of using **Bayesian statistics** to estimate the distribution of the best hyperparameters for a model. It is practically infeasible to train a model (especially those that take plenty of time) for every possible combination of hyperparameters with grid search. Yet, for continuous hyperparameters, we can only set discrete values in grid search and random search.
